title: Race and skin colour
def: The Quran makes colour and language signs of God’s creation, and no ground of superiority (49:13, 30:22).
what: “Among His signs is the creation of the heavens and the earth and the difference of your languages and colours” (30:22). “O mankind, We created you from a male and a female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another; the noblest of you with God is the most pious” (49:13). The Prophet said that no Arab is superior to a non-Arab, nor a white to a black, except by piety (Ahmad).
misread: That Muhammad was black, or that Islam is only for Arabs.
sources: Muhammad was Arab, of Quraysh; the claim that he was black has no historical basis. The first muezzin, Bilal, was an Ethiopian former slave, and the Prophet rebuked Abu Dharr for insulting a man by his mother’s blackness, saying “you are a man in whom there is ignorance” (Sahih al-Bukhari). Muslim societies have also known racism, and the teaching is a standard against which they are judged.

title: Rass, People of the
def: A people named twice in the Quran as destroyed after rejecting their prophet; who they were is not known.
what: The Quran mentions “the companions of the Rass” with Noah’s people and Thamud and ʿĀd (25:38, 50:12). Rass means a well or pit. Commentators suggest different peoples and places, and none is certain.

title: Reason and faith
def: Islam does not call for blind belief; the Quran calls on people to reflect, reason and examine claims.
what: The Quran asks: “Will they not reflect?” (47:24), “Do they not ponder?” (4:82), and says “bring your proof if you are truthful” (2:111). It uses the word for “reason” in many forms in about fifty places. Classical scholars from the Mu’tazilites to al-Ghazali and Averroes argued for reason in different ways, and the philosopher Ibn Rushd wrote that the study of nature is commanded by scripture.
sources: Schools differ on how much reason can establish apart from revelation. The Muslim position is that revelation and sound reason do not contradict, and that when they appear to, one of them has been misread.

title: Riba
def: Interest or unjust gain on loans, which the Quran forbids.
what: “God has permitted trade and forbidden riba” (2:275). The Quran warns believers to give up what remains of it (2:278–279) and not to take it “doubled and redoubled” (3:130). The Prophet cursed the one who takes it, the one who gives it, the one who writes it and the two witnesses (Sahih Muslim). The reason is that lending is a matter of kindness, and gain without risk or work lets wealth grow at the cost of the poor.
sources: Jurists debate which transactions count as riba, but all agree that fixed interest on a loan does. Islamic finance builds on partnership and sale in place of interest.
